Blog · March 2020

How to set healthy boundaries

A healthy relationship leaves both people room to be themselves and keep their integrity intact. Plenty of people end up alongside someone who treats their limits as negotiable and their own needs as the ones that matter. If holding a boundary feels almost impossible, that is usually learned rather than innate: in a chaotic or insecure household, limits get overridden often enough that you stop setting them.

Five steps

  1. Identify your limits. You cannot hold a boundary you have not worked out. Before anything is said to anyone, get clear on what you will and will not accept, what reliably drains or upsets you, and what actually makes you feel good. Vagueness here is what turns a boundary into a negotiation later.
  2. Do not be shy about saying it. People come from different families and read situations differently. An implied boundary is often simply not perceived, and the other person is not necessarily ignoring you so much as missing it entirely. Say it plainly, directly and out loud. This is uncomfortable and it is still the shortest route.
  3. Pay attention to your feelings. Your own reaction is the instrument. Notice how you feel during and after an interaction, in a journal if that helps. Resentment and anger are the reliable signals that a limit was crossed. When they turn up, restate the boundary. If it keeps being disregarded after that, withdrawing from the interaction is a legitimate response rather than a failure.
  4. Make self-care a priority. Putting your own needs first feels wrong to anyone who has spent years meeting everyone else's, and the discomfort is not evidence that you are doing something selfish. Give yourself permission to have needs and to meet them. Boundaries held out of obligation collapse; boundaries held because you believe you are allowed to have them do not.
  5. Speak with someone. If boundaries keep collapsing, the obstacle is usually not technique. It is a thin sense of your own worth, and that is hard to argue yourself out of alone. A therapist can trace where those feelings came from and work on the thinking and the behavior attached to them.

Why this is often harder than it sounds

If your limits were routinely overridden early on, the nervous system learned something practical: asserting a need costs more than absorbing the harm. That lesson does not expire on its own, and it does not respond to being told it is irrational.

This is the territory NARM works in, and it is why boundary trouble so often turns out to be developmental trauma wearing a practical disguise.

Common questions about boundaries

Why do I feel guilty every time I set a boundary?

Because guilt is what you were trained to feel. If having needs once made things worse at home, the alarm still fires when you have one, regardless of what you now believe. The guilt is a signal about your history rather than a verdict on your behavior.

What if someone keeps ignoring my boundary?

Restate it once, plainly. If it is still disregarded after that, the remaining option is to change your own exposure rather than their behavior, which may mean less contact or a different kind of contact. That is a boundary too.

Is a boundary the same thing as an ultimatum?

No. An ultimatum tries to control what the other person does. A boundary states what you will do, and it works even if they never change. If you find yourself issuing conditions and waiting to see whether they comply, that is something else.
